run.question: The payment-api pod in namespace app-101 had issues on November 20, 2026 around 13:45 UTC. What happened?

report.summary: Evidence available in this Run came only from Loki; Prometheus, Jaeger and the Kubernetes API all returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE on every attempt, so only application-log evidence exists. Observed facts: the payment-api pod payment-api-101-8486559b69-hptt7 in namespace app-101 emitted eight ERROR lines 'Failed to acquire database connection - pool exhausted' between 2026-11-20T13:46:00Z and 2026-11-20T14:44:00Z, with wait_time_ms rising to 4840 and queue_length up to 15; before that burst the same stream carried only INFO 'Payment processed successfully' lines (04:24–13:42). The service kept completing some payments during the burst (INFO success at 13:59 and 14:49), and no ERROR lines were returned after 14:44. So the observed problem is intermittent failure to obtain a database connection from an exhausted pool in payment-api, starting essentially at the reported time (first sampled error 13:46, one minute after 13:45). The database itself is never identified in any evidence: no database service appears in the Jaeger service list, Loki returned no log stream other than job=payment-api, and no metrics or Kubernetes objects were reachable. Whether the exhaustion originated in the application's pool sizing/configuration or in a slow/saturated database backend is therefore unresolved, and no root-cause object can be named.

claims.text: Pod payment-api-101-8486559b69-hptt7 (namespace app-101, job/service payment-api) logged ERROR 'Failed to acquire database connection - pool exhausted' at 13:46:00Z, 13:54:00Z, 14:03:00Z, 14:15:00Z, 14:19:00Z, 14:21:00Z, 14:31:00Z and 14:44:00Z on 2026-11-20; the reported wait_time_ms values were 1227, 2104, 1495, 2965, 4005, 4840, 2358 and 3836, with queue_length 10, 11, 8, 9, 10, 8, 15 and 5 respectively.

In the pre-incident part of the authorized window (03:41:20Z–13:46:00Z on 2026-11-20) the query {namespace="app-101"} returned 12 lines, all INFO 'Payment processed successfully' from payment-api-101-8486559b69-hptt7 (04:24, 05:04, 05:27, 05:50, 06:00, 06:34, 06:40, 11:19, 11:40, 11:44, 12:57 and 13:42); the result was not truncated, so no ERROR line was among them.

payment-api was not completely down during the error burst: INFO 'Payment processed successfully' lines were returned at 13:59:00Z (payment_id PAY-1800) and 14:49:00Z (payment_id PAY-8206) between and after the ERROR lines.

Across all namespaces, the query {namespace=~".+"} |= "\"level\": \"ERROR\"" for 12:00–15:00Z on 2026-11-20 returned only payment-api rows (8 lines, stream labels job=payment-api, namespace app-101, pod payment-api-101-8486559b69-hptt7); no other service's ERROR line was returned in that window.

The only Loki stream set returned for {job=~".+"} over the full authorized window (03:41:20Z 2026-11-20 – 03:41:20Z 2026-11-21) was 36 lines, all with labels job=payment-api, namespace app-101, pod payment-api-101-8486559b69-hptt7; in that result the last ERROR line is 14:44:00Z and later lines are INFO successes (14:49, 15:27, 17:01, 17:38, 19:25, 20:09, 21:47, 21:52, 22:19, 00:30, 00:34, 01:12, 01:39, 03:15), with the single line 'Payment API started' at 2026-11-21T03:39:56.875438Z.

A namespace-wide regex filter for pool/timeout/connection terms over 12:00–16:00Z on 2026-11-20 returned only the same 8 payment-api 'pool exhausted' ERROR lines; no database server, connection-pool size, max_connections or timeout message from any other workload or namespace was returned.

The most likely mechanism is saturation of payment-api's database connection pool: each failure is a failed acquisition after 1.2–4.8 s of waiting with a queue of 5–15 waiters, which is consistent with either a pool that is too small for the offered concurrency or a database backend that became slow/limited during 13:45–14:45. The evidence does not distinguish which: the database endpoint, its identity and its own health were never observed.

An alternative candidate cause is a change to payment-api's pool/connection configuration (for example a smaller max pool or connection limit) applied around 13:45, since the first sampled error is at 13:46 immediately after a normal success at 13:42; no configuration value, ConfigMap or change record was observable in this Run.

A further candidate that cannot be excluded is that the database backend itself refused or slowed acquisitions (server-side connection limit or latency), because no database logs, database metrics or dependency spans were available; the payment-api messages only state that the pool was exhausted, not why connections were not returned or replenished.

A crash/restart or container replacement of the payment-api pod at ~13:45 as the direct trigger is not supported by the log evidence: within the 36 lines returned for the whole authorized window the only 'Payment API started' line is 2026-11-21T03:39:56.875438Z, about 14 hours after the incident, and the pod name payment-api-101-8486559b69-hptt7 is unchanged before, during and after the burst (caveat: the log stream is sparse and Kubernetes pod/restart status was unreachable, so restart counts are unverified).

Inspect the payment-api deployment's database connection-pool configuration (pool size, acquisition timeout, idle/leak settings in its ConfigMap/env) and the database backend's connection limit and latency for 13:45–14:45Z on 2026-11-20, since the pool-exhaustion errors name the pool but the evidence never identifies the database or the configured limit.

Re-run the Prometheus, Jaeger and Kubernetes checks once those sources are reachable: payment-api error rate by status_code, rpc/http latency, pod restart counts and last termination reason, events in app-101, and ConfigMap contents for the pool settings, to decide between pool sizing, a config change and database-side saturation.

gaps: Prometheus was unreachable in this Run: get_metric_names, metrics_range_query and execute_prometheus_instant_query all returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, so no error-rate, request-latency, connection-pool, saturation or kube-state series for payment-api (or any service) could be read; missing series are unknown, not zero.

Jaeger was unreachable: traces_list_services and traces_search returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, so no span status, operation-level latency or parent-child call edge to a database dependency could be established.

The Kubernetes API was unreachable: kubernetes_jq_query, kubernetes_count and kubernetes_tabular_query all returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, so pod phase, container restart count, last termination reason, OOMKilled/Evicted events, deployment→ReplicaSet→pod ownership, and events across namespaces could not be checked.

The identity, configuration and health of the database that payment-api could not get a connection from are unknown; no database log stream, metric or span was returned, and secrets could not be read, so whether the pool size, the acquisition timeout or the database side caused the exhaustion is unverified.
The change_history integration is not integrated in this Run, so no change record around 2026-11-20T13:45:00Z could be consulted for a configuration or deployment change.

Loki returned only the job=payment-api stream (36 lines over the whole authorized window, roughly one line every few minutes), so the absence of ERROR lines for other services or after 14:44 is limited to what these queries matched and is not proof that nothing else failed.

Queries for 'pool exhausted' before 13:45 and for error text after 14:45 returned no data (status no_data), which shows only that those queries matched nothing, so the exact start time (13:45 vs first sampled 13:46) and the exact end of the burst are unconfirmed.

A 'Payment API started' log line at 2026-11-21T03:39:56.875438Z appears after the incident window; whether it reflects a container restart, and whether restart counts changed during the incident, cannot be determined without Kubernetes access.
next_steps: Read the payment-api Deployment/ConfigMap for the database pool settings (max pool size, acquisition timeout, leak detection) and compare with the values in effect before 13:45Z on 2026-11-20 if a change record is available.

Check the database backend's own metrics and logs (connection count, max_connections, wait/latency) for 13:45–14:45Z to determine whether the pool exhaustion was caused by backend saturation or by payment-api's pool sizing.

Once Kubernetes and Prometheus are reachable, verify pod restart counts, last termination reason and events for payment-api-101-8486559b69-hptt7, and read payment-api error rate/latency by status_code around 13:45Z to quantify the impact on callers.
